lead: This unit shows how a vision system turns pixels into repeatable features, then uses geometry and motion to recover where cameras and objects are. You start with corners and descriptors, build image-level representations, then move to camera models, stereo, structure from motion, optical flow and registration. After it you can design a feature-matching pipeline, calibrate a camera, estimate depth or motion, and align two images.
about: The unit moves from local evidence to global geometry. Chapter 5.1 detects corners and blobs with the Harris detector; 5.2 turns keypoints into SIFT and SURF descriptors; 5.3 and 5.4 make fixed-length and word-based image representations with HOG and bag of visual words. Chapter 5.5 introduces the pinhole camera and calibration. Chapter 5.6 explains epipolar geometry and stereo depth; 5.7 extends this to structure from motion and 3D reconstruction. Chapter 5.8 estimates pixel motion with optical flow; 5.9 aligns images with registration. Each chapter uses earlier filters, edges and transforms, and feeds later recognition or medical imaging work.

chapters.idea: A corner is a point whose local intensity changes in two directions; Harris turns that test into a small matrix and a scalar response.
chapters.depth: Visual features: edges, corners, blobs. Harris detector: image gradients Ix, Iy; window sum; structure matrix H = Σ w [Ix² IxIy; IxIy Iy²]; eigenvalues λ1, λ2; response R = det H − k(trace H)² with k ≈ 0.04; non-maximum suppression; threshold. Shi-Tomasi uses R = λmin. Blob detection by LoG/DoG at scales as a short bridge. Some syllabi call H the second-moment matrix. Mention Harris is rotation invariant but not scale invariant.

figure.title: Harris detector
figure.aria: Flow of the Harris detector from image gradients to the structure matrix, response map and non-maximum suppression.

chapters.example: A 2×2 window has Ix = [2, 2; −2, −2] and Iy = [2, −2; 2, −2], equal weights. Find H, eigenvalues and Harris response with k = 0.04. Solution: Σ Ix² = 16, Σ Iy² = 16, Σ IxIy = 0, so H = [[16, 0], [0, 16]]. Eigenvalues are 16 and 16. det H = 256, trace H = 32, R = 256 − 0.04 × 32² = 256 − 40.96 = 215.04. Both eigenvalues are large, so the point is a corner.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to sum over the window, or using the response without non-maximum suppression. A single-pixel H can label noise as a corner; Harris is not scale invariant.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 convolution and gradients; Unit 4 edges.
chapters.leave: Scale-space SIFT in 5.2; matching and RANSAC in 5.4 and 5.7; Hough transform to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: SIFT and SURF describe a keypoint by local gradient patterns so matches survive scale, rotation and small viewpoint changes.
chapters.depth: Scale space; Difference of Gaussians; keypoint localization and contrast threshold; orientation assignment; 128-D SIFT descriptor (4×4 cells × 8 bins); normalization and clipping. SURF: box-filter Hessian approximation, Haar wavelets, 64-D descriptor, upright variant. Ratio test for matching. Some syllabi call this scale-invariant feature extraction. Only a few universities teach SURF's integral-image speed details; keep them short.

figure.title: SIFT pipeline
figure.aria: SIFT pipeline from scale space to keypoints, orientation assignment and the final descriptor.

chapters.example: A SIFT orientation cell gives 4-bin counts [1, 3, 0, 2]. Normalize the vector in L2 norm. Solution: norm = √(1² + 3² + 0² + 2²) = √14 = 3.742. Normalized vector = [0.267, 0.802, 0, 0.534] (rounded). In full SIFT, 16 such cells give 128 values, followed by clipping and renormalization.
chapters.trap: Treating raw histogram counts as the descriptor; SIFT smooths the orientation histogram and normalizes the descriptor. SURF is not just a faster SIFT; its descriptor and detector differ.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 keypoints; Unit 2 image pyramids and Gaussian filtering; Unit 4 gradients.
chapters.leave: Descriptor matching, RANSAC and vocabulary building to 5.4 and 5.7; CNN features to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: HOG describes local shape by counting gradient directions in cells and normalizing over blocks.
chapters.depth: Gradient magnitude and orientation; unsigned orientation bins (classic 9 bins over 0°–180°); cells; overlapping blocks; block normalization (L2-Hys); sliding-window detection; use in pedestrian detection. Compare with SIFT: HOG is dense, with no keypoint detector. Mention LBP as a related texture descriptor in some syllabi; keep LBP to one line.

figure.title: HOG descriptor
figure.aria: HOG pipeline from gradients to cell histograms, block normalization and the final HOG vector.

chapters.example: One 8×8 cell has four gradient samples (angle, magnitude): (10°, 2), (50°, 1), (110°, 3), (170°, 2). Use 9 unsigned bins of 20° with no interpolation. Build the histogram and L2-normalize it. Solution: bins 1 to 9 are [2, 0, 1, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 2]. Norm = √(4 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 9 + 0 + 0 + 4) = √18 = 4.243. Normalized = [0.471, 0, 0.236, 0, 0, 0.707, 0, 0, 0.471].
chapters.trap: Using signed orientation when the detector expects unsigned; misplacing 170° near 0°; forgetting block normalization. A cell histogram alone is not the final HOG descriptor.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 gradients and edges; 5.2 local descriptors.
chapters.leave: Classifier training to Unit 6; LBP details to texture study in Unit 1/4; optical flow to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Bag of visual words turns many local descriptors into a fixed-length histogram by clustering them into a visual vocabulary.
chapters.depth: Local descriptors from 5.2; k-means vocabulary with k words; assignment to nearest word; histogram; tf-idf weighting; spatial pyramid matching; VLAD as a compact extension; classifier such as k-NN or SVM (only mention). Some syllabi call this bag-of-words or BoVW. Keep the VLAD formula short.

figure.title: BoVW pipeline
figure.aria: Bag-of-visual-words pipeline from local descriptors to vocabulary, word assignment and image histogram.

chapters.example: A vocabulary has k = 3 words. An image's six descriptors are assigned to words [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]. Build the normalized histogram. Solution: counts are word 1 = 2, word 2 = 1, word 3 = 3. Total = 6. Normalized histogram = [2/6, 1/6, 3/6] = [0.333, 0.167, 0.500].
chapters.trap: Recomputing k-means for every test image; forgetting that word order is arbitrary but fixed after training. A BoVW histogram loses spatial layout unless a pyramid is added.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 SIFT/SURF; basic clustering and classifiers from Unit 6 (k-NN, SVM).
chapters.leave: Classifier details to Unit 6; RANSAC to 5.7; VLAD coding details advanced only.

chapters.idea: A pinhole camera maps 3D points to pixels through intrinsic and extrinsic matrices, and calibration finds those numbers.
chapters.depth: Pinhole model; perspective projection; homogeneous coordinates; intrinsic matrix K with focal lengths fx, fy and principal point (cx, cy); extrinsic rotation R and translation t; world-to-camera; radial and tangential distortion; checkerboard calibration; DLT and Zhang's method (only a few universities teach Zhang's closed-form steps in detail); reprojection error. Some syllabi call this camera resection.

figure.title: Pinhole projection
figure.aria: Pinhole projection from a world point through extrinsic rotation and translation, then the intrinsic matrix, to a pixel.

chapters.example: A camera has fx = fy = 800 px, cx = 320 px, cy = 240 px. A point in camera coordinates is (X, Y, Z) = (1.0 m, 0.5 m, 2.0 m). Find its pixel (u, v). Solution: u = fx X/Z + cx = 800 × 1.0/2.0 + 320 = 720 px. v = fy Y/Z + cy = 800 × 0.5/2.0 + 240 = 440 px.
chapters.trap: Using focal length in millimetres inside K; forgetting to divide by Z; mixing world and camera coordinates. Extrinsic maps world to camera before K.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 image formation; matrix multiplication and homogeneous coordinates.
chapters.leave: Epipolar geometry and stereo to 5.6; distortion fitting details to lab.

chapters.idea: Two views of the same point constrain each other to epipolar lines; this gives depth and camera motion.
chapters.depth: Epipole; epipolar plane and line; essential matrix E for normalized coordinates; fundamental matrix F for pixels; x2ᵀ F x1 = 0; eight-point algorithm with RANSAC (only a few universities teach the full derivation); stereo rectification; disparity d; depth Z = f B / d with baseline B and focal f; triangulation; multi-view projective geometry. Some syllabi call F the bifocal tensor.

figure.aria: Two camera centers C1 and C2 see a 3D point X; its projections x1 and x2 lie on corresponding epipolar lines through epipoles e1 and e2.

chapters.example: A rectified stereo pair has focal length f = 800 px and baseline B = 0.12 m. A point has disparity d = 24 px. Find depth Z. Solution: Z = f B / d = 800 × 0.12 / 24 = 4.0 m.
chapters.trap: Swapping F and E; using disparity in metres instead of pixels; forgetting that rectified images are needed for Z = fB/d. F uses pixels, E uses normalized camera coordinates.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 camera model and intrinsic matrix; linear algebra.
chapters.leave: SfM and bundle adjustment to 5.7; dense stereo algorithms to lab.

chapters.idea: Structure from motion recovers camera poses and 3D points together from many images.
chapters.depth: Feature tracks; two-view initialization; triangulation; perspective-n-point (PnP); incremental SfM; bundle adjustment minimizing reprojection error; sparse vs dense reconstruction; multi-view stereo. Only a few universities teach bundle adjustment in detail; keep the normal equations short. Some syllabi call this 3D structure and motion estimation.

figure.title: Incremental SfM
figure.aria: Incremental structure from motion from features and tracks to two-view initialization, adding views by PnP and bundle adjustment.

chapters.example: Two calibrated cameras look along +Z. C1 = (0, 0, 0), C2 = (1, 0, 0) m. A point has normalized image coordinates u1 = 0.2 in camera 1 and u2 = −0.1 in camera 2; both v = 0. Find X and Z. Solution: u1 = X/Z, u2 = (X − B)/Z with B = 1 m. Subtract: u1 − u2 = B/Z, so Z = B/(u1 − u2) = 1/0.3 = 3.333 m. X = u1 Z = 0.2 × 3.333 = 0.667 m. The 3D point is (0.667, 0, 3.333) m.
chapters.trap: Monocular SfM has unknown scale; bundle adjustment minimizes reprojection error, not Euclidean 3D error. Poor tracks break initialization.
chapters.leave: Dense multi-view stereo and deep learned SfM to lab/Unit 6; camera calibration to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Optical flow estimates per-pixel motion between frames using brightness constancy and smoothness.
chapters.depth: Motion field vs optical flow; brightness constancy; gradient equation Ix u + Iy v + It = 0; aperture problem; Lucas-Kanade local least squares; Horn-Schunck global smoothness (only a few universities teach the variational derivation); pyramids for large motion; applications. Some syllabi call this motion estimation.

figure.title: Lucas-Kanade flow
figure.aria: Lucas-Kanade optical flow from two frames and spatiotemporal gradients to window least squares and a flow vector.

chapters.example: Two pixels in a window give brightness equations: pixel A has (Ix, Iy, It) = (2, 0, 1); pixel B has (0, 2, 1). Solve Lucas-Kanade for flow (u, v) in pixels/frame. Solution: 2u + 0v + 1 = 0 → u = −0.5. 0u + 2v + 1 = 0 → v = −0.5. Flow = (−0.5, −0.5) px/frame; magnitude = √(0.5² + 0.5²) = 0.707 px/frame.
chapters.trap: Using one pixel equation for two unknowns; confusing optical flow with true object motion. Brightness changes and occlusions break the constancy assumption.
chapters.leave: Video action recognition to Unit 6; dense variational details advanced.

chapters.idea: Registration finds a spatial transform that aligns one image to another.
chapters.depth: Fixed and moving images; transform types translation, rigid, affine, projective, nonrigid; feature-based registration with keypoints and RANSAC; intensity-based registration with similarity metrics SSD, NCC and mutual information for multimodal medical images; optimizer; interpolation; resampling; evaluation by overlap or target registration error. Mention DICOM/PACS/NIfTI only as medical file context. Some syllabi call this image alignment.

figure.title: Registration loop
figure.aria: Registration loop where fixed and moving images meet at a transform, a similarity metric drives an optimizer that updates the transform, producing an aligned image.

chapters.example: Three corresponding points are moving (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) and fixed (1,1), (3,1), (1,3). Find the affine transform that maps moving to fixed in homogeneous form. Solution: x_fixed = 2x_moving + 1, y_fixed = 2y_moving + 1, so the matrix is [[2, 0, 1], [0, 2, 1], [0, 0, 1]].
chapters.trap: Choosing a transform with too few degrees of freedom; using SSD for images with different brightness or modalities. Registration maps moving to fixed, so direction matters.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 geometric operations and interpolation; 5.2 feature matching.
chapters.leave: Image fusion is outside this unit; optical flow to 5.8; deep registration to Unit 6.
